author: Semhal Meles Zenawi
title: Ethiopia: Elections, Constitutional Change, and Genocidal Violence
content:
In November 2020, a war erupted in the Ethiopian region of Tigray. Six hundred thousand to a million civilian lives are estimated to have been lost. Amongst the many war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during the two-year war was genocide against Tigrayans. Abiy Ahmed has on several occasions insisted that the catalyst for war was his intolerance for voluntary disassociation and the exercise of the right to vote. 




The National Electoral Board of Ethiopia (NEBE) postponed the 2020 election several times, but the final “indefinite” postponement under the cover of COVID-19 breached the constitutionally set term limit. Then NEBE chair Birtukan Mideksa’s claim that COVID-19 introduced public health imperatives that overrode those of democracy was unconvincing given the government’s non-enforcement of other measures such as lockdowns or even social distancing, and its farcical claim of having developed a “homegrown” cure. 




Following a public outcry over the “corona-clouded power grab”, four prescriptive options for a “constitutional route to postponement” were presented to a curated array of government-aligned opposition by the then minister of justice, now minister of foreign affairs, Gedion Timothewos. The exercise was met with derision, even by its hand-selected participants. An equally performative constitutional “tribunal” was held, but that too failed to foster agreement over the legality of the postponement and the legitimacy of the government following the expiration of its term. 




Having catalysed constitutional chaos, Mideksa set about facilitating Ahmed’s bypassing of various laws and bylaws to dissolve the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF) and establish the Prosperity Party (PP). Beyond legal and procedural controversies, the move to reconstitute the EPRDF drew criticism for its intent. Abiy’s desire to dissolve the EPRDF and 

“Medemer”

 (amalgamate) its constituent and affiliated parts was viewed by many as an initial step towards constitutional remaking and a reversal of multinational federalism.




The dissolution of the EPRDF ended the “reformist” coalition known as Team Lemma that propelled Abiy Ahmed to its chairmanship and Ethiopia’s prime ministership. In August 2020, Lemma Megersa, after whom Team Lemma was named, was removed from the Prosperity Party and as Minister of Defence for opposing the EPRDF’s amalgamation. The PP’s establishment was so ad hoc that it remains unclear if Megersa had actually joined the PP before he was booted out.




The relationship between the erstwhile allies came under strain as early as 2019 and was indicative of a wider rift between Abiy Ahmed and his Oromo base over the meaning of “reform” and its alignment with the demands of the protests that spurred Team Lemma’s rise. Ahmed positioned himself as an Oromo populist championing the cause of the Oromo farmer and, more broadly, seeking the “proper implementation of federalism”. Once in power, he started to appeal to a form of “pan-Ethiopian” nationalism which hoped to homogenize national identity and recentralize Ethiopia’s governing structures. Many in Ahmed’s Oromo base viewed the turn as a betrayal of the cause. Even before Megersa’s political downfall, suspicions over Ahmed’s intentions ignited a still-raging conflict with the Oromo Liberation Army. 




For a time, Abiy managed to force together the antagonistic nationalisms by offering a shared enemy – Tigrayan supremacy. Once considered the champion of the “national question”, the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) was recast as the primary impediment to its “proper implementation”, while maintaining its long-held position as the primary impediment to the return of a unitary institutional setup. “Tigrinya speakers” became “daytime hyenas” on whom the country’s many political and social crises could be scapegoated. 




The TPLF opposed the postponement of the election and refused to recognize the federal government once its constitutionally set term was over. Unfortunately, the TPLF did not lodge an official challenge to the postponement through its seats in both chambers of parliament. Instead, it retreated into Tigray to shore up its base and made plans to hold a regional election within constitutionally set limits.




Both the dissolution of the EPRDF and the postponement of the elections drew widespread criticism from divergent opposition groups. Still, the TPLF’s concerns were dismissed as the mere disgruntlements of “hardline old guard (…) bad losers” piqued to see their star waning after being displaced from power, and jealous of the neoliberal “reforms” and “peacemaking” of the new prime minister. The perniciousness of this view all but excluded serious discussion over the democratic merits of Ahmed’s neoliberal reforms, their compatibility with the governing structures of Ethiopia, and the processes and procedures through which said structures should or could be altered without reverting to violence. 




Most analysts explain Abiy’s centralizing impulse as a personal problem: a desire to fulfil his mother’s prophecy that “my son, you will be king”; a religious conviction – pastors say he is the messiah; a need to fill the gaping hole left by a philandering absentee father, all of which, we are told, made him look back towards Ethiopia’s imperialist past. Through this lens, genocide becomes a way for Ahmed to work out his “daddy issues”. While I don’t doubt Ahmed’s delusions of grandeur, or the international community’s benevolence, it is unlikely they underwrote genocide to help Ahmed cope with his personal pathologies. 




One of the many “heroic assumptions” underlying the neoliberal reforms Ahmed instituted is the existence of a unified state with a homogenized identity. None exists in Ethiopia; our history won’t allow for it. The economic inequalities generally associated with neoliberal reform have put such pressure on societal cohesion and nation building – even in states without the historical baggage or ethnic plurality of Ethiopia – as to lead to their failure. African history over the last half century is replete with examples. Ethiopia’s governing structures, designed on the basis of its historical idiosyncrasies rather than abstract theories formulated in Chicago, are in obvious friction with the dictates of the IMF and the World Bank. Centralizing Ethiopia was, for this reason, always going to be a violent affair. The international community’s workaround was to encourage the PP’s brutal infringements on the rights and liberties of Ethiopian citizens by framing tyranny as exclusively and excusably aimed at the TPLF. 




NEBE enjoyed unwavering diplomatic support, most directly expressed through the United Nations Development Programme’s (UNDP) “Supporting Elections for Ethiopia’s Democratic Strengthening” (SEEDS) project. The project, and its successor SEEDS II, were both explicitly designed to strengthen the institutional capacity of NEBE to conduct 

“credible, inclusive, transparent, and peaceful elections”.

 The reforms funded by SEEDS have yet to achieve these objectives. What we have seen instead is an increased entanglement between ballots and bullets.




Mideksa’s personal commitment to using elections as instruments of genocide led her to resign in protest at the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement (CoHA) that brought the war to a formal end in November 2022. She, like many in the “pan-Ethiopian” camp, viewed Ahmed’s failure to “finish off the Tigrayans” as a setback to the return of the unitary state including now independent Eritrea. She need not have fretted. The 2026 election cycle triggered war and cemented the relationship between the two. 




The agreements ending the 2020–2022 genocide litigated the constitutional interpretations that led to the war. The government established through Tigray’s regional election was deemed illegitimate and disbanded. Setting aside the moral implication of overturning elections through genocide, the dissolution of government meant Tigray would go without a legislative branch, and its constitution would, in effect, be suspended. The agreements became the legal thread tying Tigray to the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia until an election restored the constitutional order. This created significant institutional gaps within Tigray and its relationship to the rest of the federation. To bridge some of these gaps, CoHA stipulated an interim administration whose cabinet would be formed on the basis of negotiations between the TPLF and the federal government.




Initially, the federal government showed little interest in the establishment of the Tigray Interim Regional Administration (TIRA), and Tigrayan political elites debated its composition without interference. Abiy Ahmed began to take an interest in the appointment of the president, vetoing TPLF chairperson Debretsion Gebremichael and all the other members of the TPLF’s Executive Committee (EC). Ahmed demanded that a “new face” take charge of the interim setup. Following instructions, the EC coalesced around Fiseha Haftetsion, a young technocratic member of the Central Committee (CC) as their preferred candidate. The TPLF’s CC overrode the EC, selecting Getachew Reda for the presidency with a narrow majority. Abiy’s acceptance of the TPLF’s selection despite his earlier dismissal of members of the EC raised suspicions amongst Reda’s comrades in the party’s highest decision-making organ, exacerbating the distrust that emerged from his role in the opaque negotiations that led to COHA. 




These suspicions were heightened when Ahmed appointed Reda president through Intervention Proclamation 359/2003 rather than through the modalities built on the basis of the CoHA. Every extension of TIRA’s mandate and the accompanying presidential “appointment” invoked Intervention Proclamation 359/2003. Bypassing CoHA through a proclamation designed to regulate military intervention in regional states was a worrisome indication of the Prosperity regime’s intentions. Intentions aside, given that Tigray has yet to reintegrate into the Ethiopian federation, it is unclear whether Tigray is bound by Intervention Proclamation 359/2003, or any other federal laws.




Reda sought to leverage the wartime camaraderie he had established with the generals of the Tigray Defense Forces (TDF) to counter his political isolation within the EC. Upon his insistence, active-duty combatants and non-TPLF members of TIRA were invited to participate in the meetings held from November to December 2022 to evaluate party leadership during the war. Reda’s gambit backfired; Fetlework Gebregziabher, his most ardent critic in the EC, emerged as the generals’ darling. Despite concluding by appointing him the TPLF’s deputy chairman, the November/December evaluations triggered a snail-paced coup that held Reda at gunpoint until his ouster and exile.




Following the November/December 2022 evaluation meetings, Fetlework Gebregziabher quickly manoeuvred to consolidate her hold on the TPLF through a party congress. Tensions hit fever pitch as the Prosperity regime, backing Reda, insisted a congress could only take place under the auspices of NEBE and that the latter had no intention of accommodating the congress. The TPLF went ahead with the congress, which Reda and his faction boycotted, arguing that the party had not adhered to national election law or its own bylaws. Reda decided to boycott despite retaining support from important party organs such as the congress oversight committee, thereby delegitimizing the only processes, however flawed, that could have reestablished the primacy of the political. 




The TPLF pointed to NEBE’s two-year-long foot-dragging over the reinstatement of its legal registration, initially voided in January 2021 following the outbreak of war, as evidence of its bias and desire to undermine CoHA. The TPLF argued that failing to recognize the legality of a signatory to the agreement amounted to its nullification. Nullifying CoHA, as the TPLF claims NEBE did, would sever the last remaining legal tie between Tigray and the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia. Given that Tigray’s own constitution remains suspended until it elects a legislative wing, legally speaking, the region no longer exists.




Having essentially declared martial law on dubious legal grounds, Ahmed went about stripping Tigray of a legal identity. NEBE’s decision marked a souring of TPLF’s relationship with itself, the interim government, and the prosperity regime. It all but assured that Tigray would remain in legal limbo for the entirety of the 2020–2026 term of government.  




The failure to fully reintegrate Tigray and the attempt at stripping it of a legal identity are the driving factors of Pretoria’s inability to make political gains on – and sustain – peace. Processes such as the reinstatement of Tigray’s constitutional borders, the return of Internally Displaced Persons, and Disarmament, Demobilization and Reintegration, all of which had initially shown promise, stalled as they became subject to differences over institutional arrangements. Some would argue that, given that regional states can essentially veto constitutional amendments, and Abiy has plans to amend the constitution, leaving Tigray in legal limbo suits his agenda just fine. The decision to exclude Tigray from the 2026 election all but assured the outbreak of war if for no other reason than that the terms of our union with Ethiopia are being altered without our consent. 




Ahmed’s unilateral extension of TIRA’s term two months before a national election set to exclude Tigray was met by the TPLF’s restitution of Tigray’s pre-war council. The restitution of the council reimposed the TPLF’s monopoly over Tigray’s political space, but it also put its constitution back into play and gave it access to a legislative arm, however illegitimate, through which it was      trying to address some of the institutional and legal gaps. 




A few days after the election, Ahmed oversaw the opening of a congress organized by the Ethiopian National Dialogue Commission. The commission was established in late 2021 as Tigray Defence Forces made significant military gains that threatened the capital. Despite the language of national reconciliation that informed its establishment, many felt the commission was an attempt at concentrating power in the person of Abiy Ahmed and bypassing constitutional ends towards constitutional change. The conference was to serve as the culmination of the commission’s work and was expected to roll out the basis for Ethiopia’s transition into a unitary state and a presidential system. Various changes to the electoral system anticipating this shift had quietly been rolled out in the 2026 election with no public debate or oversight. 




Instead, the conference revealed Ahmed’s waning power. The changes Ahmed wanted were in effect vetoed by members of his ruling party organizing around Shimelis Abdisa, the president of Oromia region. Abdisa seems to have been able to galvanize support not just from within the Prosperity Party, but from an Oromo opposition that had grown weary of Abiy Ahmed. Whatever their perhaps theatrical differences on constitutional change, messaging from opposition actors aligned to Abdisa suggests his alignment with Ahmed on the issue of war with “the northerners”.




To bolster his waning popularity and, apparently, his inability to effectively project power in his own party, Ahmed fell back on a familiar formula – anti-Tigrayan populism. On 31 July, Ahmed appeared on Amhara state television bemoaning that Fano, a conglomeration of Amhara militia groups allied to him during the genocide, were now allied with the TPLF. Their alliance with the TPLF, he claimed, was built on Fano agreeing to drop their claims to Western Tigray. The Ethiopian National Defense Force attacked a TDF camp in Western Tigray, close to the Sudanese border, on August 1st. 




The split with Fano occurred when they were left out of the negotiations that led to CoHA, an agreement they felt undermined them by calling for their disarmament and the return of Tigray’s constitutionally mandated borders. The return of “ancestral lands” had been a rallying cry of Amhara nationalism, and was sold as a central aim of the 2020–2022 war. Ahmed’s decision to “betray the cause” may have been motivated by his plans to satisfy populist appetites through the conquest of Assab in Eritrea and/or Berbera in Somalia. A few days later, he appeared on Oromo state television to claim that he would return Oromo ancestral lands in Eritrea. The PP regime is open about plans to use the return of war in Tigray as an opportunity to “alter geography”.       




The argument laid out to legitimize the conquest of Assab, if not Berbera, is based on a rejection of the process through which Eritrea formally achieved independence, that is, the process that established the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia on the ashes of the Provisional Military Government of Socialist Ethiopia. There is, then, an explicit link between the desire for constitutional change and territorial expansion. 




Whatever the merits of the arguments against the transitional period of the early ’90s, it is important to note that the governing structures of Ethiopia have since been legitimized by seven election cycles, including three that, in the final accounting, delivered Abiy Ahmed the prime ministership. It is to be recalled that Ahmed unleashed genocide on his citizens, with his Eritrean partners, under the guise of a “law enforcement operation” to defend Ethiopia’s constitution.




On 8 August, with Tigray in the midst of sustained aerial attacks, Debretsion Gebremichael held a presser adding Ahmed’s plans to “rip up” the constitution to the list of reasons Pretoria, which maintained constitutional signposts, was dead. In the same presser, Gebremichael made public the formation of an “Alliance for Survival”, a still growing grouping of armed Ethiopian actors with a shared mission of overthrowing the prosperity regime. The Alliance for Survival too has plans to “rip up” the constitution. In their first shared statement, Alliance members used the constitutional language of “Nations, nationalities, and peoples of Ethiopia”, but let it be known that the regime rests on an “anti-people state structure” which would be replaced through an “honest, trustworthy, fully inclusive and participatory popular and constitutional dialogue”.




Shortly after issuing the statement, a section within TDF took over federal installations in Tigray, including three airports, and launched an offensive that dislodged it from the Tigrayan capital and returned, yet again, to its insurgent roots.




Ahmed celebrated his conquest of Mekelle by hosting a gala to announce that the Commission’s recommendations would be presented to parliament for ratification. The expectation is that Tigray’s lack of a legal identity and elected council, in concomitance with its lack of representation in both chambers of parliament at the federal level, means he can change the terms of Tigray’s belonging to the federation while the regional state is in legal purgatory.




While the likes of Birtukan Mideksa hoped that the 2020–2022 war would end with a return of the unitary Ethiopian state, both sides, at least rhetorically, sought to uphold their interpretation of the constitution. The start of war in 2026 threatens to make the country the epicentre of a theatre of war stretching from the Sahel to Iran and is explicitly about undoing the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia. What comes next is anybody’s guess. Still, whatever wars are won or lost, and however entangled they become, the right to vote remains inviolable and inalienable. Given that Tigrayans have been denied the right to vote for six years, Tigray cannot be legally or morally beholden to changes to the terms of its constitutional relationship with Ethiopia imposed by either belligerent of the war on Tigray.

author: Leonard Wanyama
title: Misuse of the Tax Commissioner General’s Powers is Hurting Kenyans
content:
As I sat there listening to a friend who owns a small business, I wondered whether there are different tax regimes in Kenya depending on what form of commercial activity one undertakes.




Despite working in tax advocacy for the past nine years, this was the first time I was coming across a VAT Withholding Tax (henceforth referred to as VWT). 




Indeed, this is something different from what is generally understood as Value-Added Tax (VAT) and the fact that many small businesses are finding themselves being ambushed by it goes to show how much Kenyan taxation requires a lot more democracy.




VAT is the standard rate of 16 per cent tax that is charged on the consumption of goods and services supplied or purchased. Businesses charge it as part of the cost, then remit the difference between the price and the tariff to the government. Every good or service, from fuel to bread, usually has a 16 per cent cost added to it.




The VWT, on the other hand, is a mechanism to collect VAT at the point of supplies provision. This means that for selected businesses, there is a tax within a tax for every purchase they make. In this case, the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) appoints selected businesses or individual entities as their agents to deduct this tax at a fixed rate of 2 per cent on the advance payment to their suppliers.




Essentially, once the supplier gives you the price of a good or service inclusive of 16 per cent VAT, if you are appointed a KRA agent to implement VWT, you would hold on to 2 per cent of that payment for remittance to the tax collector. 




This must then be reconciled through the electronic Tax Invoice Management System (eTIMS). The system has unfortunately been experiencing frequent partial or full downtimes in recent months, preventing transaction matching between sellers and buyers for accurate KRA determination of tax demands or claims.

 




My friend had no idea how his business had been selected to become a KRA implementing agent. Moreover, even when he could not reconcile the taxes using eTIMS due to frequent system downtimes, his business was still automatically liable for penalties due to noncompliance. 




This happened because even as the eTIMS system was partially shut down, other functioning segments of the tax software platform continued accumulating taxes from other regular purchases he transacted, and recorded them onto the eTIMS portal as he carried out other business. 




This revelation by my friend was to me mind-boggling because I could immediately see the tense and awkward haggling that could harm a business relationship given the current difficult commercial environment. 




Such are the tribulations small businesses are facing on top of tax contestations around cash flow mismatches, informal supply chain problems, eTIMS-related costs due to system glitches, invoicing evidence rules, and digital literacy demands for revenue compliance.




Looking at 

Section 42 of the Tax Procedures Act of 2015

, it emerges that the application of the law in this instance is vague, thereby conferring unfettered discretionary powers on public officials under the authority of the KRA Commissioner General.




There are no objective criteria as to how VWT agents are determined and these appointments then come across as arbitrary decisions that not only confuse taxpayers but also leave them paralytically unable to predict the legal consequences of their actions.




It came as no surprise a few weeks later that traders had become angry over another tax that consolidated cargo clearance charges. Though separate from the VWT issue, the manner of application of this tax is annoyingly similar.




This has resulted in 

protests by traders

 that have forced President William Ruto to order a 

review of customs costs

 and differentiated implementation in the handling of ordinary consignments compared to high-value cargo. 




This means that containers carrying commercial merchandise, everyday consumer items, bulk or general cargo of low value will continue to pay KSh 2 million for clearance. 




Meanwhile, shipments of luxury goods, specialized electronics, high-end motor vehicles, and industrial machinery will undergo further assessment based on the value of the goods in the container, which is likely to raise costs.




The two examples above are a stark reminder of Professor Migai Akech’s treatise on the 

undemocratic application of administrative law

 in taxation, where power is abused and not practised based on the principles of equity, fair treatment, and accountability.




Politically, this transforms taxation into an oppressive tool that can break into anyone’s piggy bank at any time to attain undisclosed national budgetary goals or 

silence dissenting voices

 at the whim of the powers that be, a “preserve of autocratic governance” in which Kenya is governed as a tyrannical barony.




As a result, tax collection becomes inefficient because citizens are dissuaded from active compliance due to their distrust of established policies or processes.




Despite their willingness to pay taxes – as captured in research by Twaweza East Africa on 

Taxing Matters

 – and their being aware of the publicized intent for revenue collection measures to help settle debt obligations and service delivery demands, Kenyans are sceptical of tax authorities because they do not deem them to be fair.




Kenya’s National Taxpayers Association (NTA) points out in its 

2025 Tax Perception Survey Report

 that informal sector inclusion is highly contested, resulting in lingering pessimism because KRA is viewed as obstructive while its officers are perceived as dismissive and unhelpful in explaining tax law and the accompanying regulatory demands.




This is compounded by underlying grievances such as awareness of tax avoidance and fraudulent financial practices like corruption or theft that are not properly punished within the context of poor economic growth as captured by the East African Tax and Governance Network (EATGN) in the 

2021 Kenya National Tax Outlook Survey

.




With this in mind, how then can it be that anyone can simply be ambushed to become a KRA agent without a clearly stated legal mechanism categorizing taxpayers and clearly ascertaining their legal obligations for such roles?




First, this flies in the face of the right to fair administrative action under Article 47 of the Constitution, thereby making it an unrelatable process that comes off as a whimsical application of the law.




This is because it haphazardly changes the taxpayer’s legal obligations by designating roles which simultaneously expose one to compliance costs, penalties, interest, and unforeseen duties without clear justification, prior notice, consultation, or explanation of the criteria applied in the appointment of a VWT agent. 




Secondly, it is an unscrupulous transfer of costs and other administrative burdens to private entities, thereby infringing on the right to property under Article 40 of the Constitution, where incomes are broadly protected as “

property of any description

”.




In this instance, appointed agents deploy time (explaining processes at length to their fellow taxpayers who would obviously feel shortchanged discussing tax complexity while bargaining over margins with a non-state entity), resources, personnel, and finance systems without compensation based on unclear statutes.




Thirdly, Section 23A of the Tax Procedures Act disproportionately targets small businesses while Section 23A (3a) specifically shifts responsibility from suppliers to purchasers.




The VWT, therefore, adversely affects commercial activities at a small or micro level; in remote areas with poor internet access; for those trading informally or operating with limited digital literacy – for example, the elderly; and for those that cannot afford hardware or software upgrades.




A straight line can therefore be drawn between the negative public sentiment against eTIMS and the problem of how the current application of tax systems is not only inconvenient and prohibitive but is also punishingly expensive for small businesses or traders.




This is because it is inconsistent with the constitutional right to equality and freedom from discrimination under Article 27(1) of the constitution that guarantees that eTIMS application should offer equal protection and benefits under the law. Furthermore, Article 27(4) prohibits direct or indirect discrimination.




One must ask: how does a purchaser generate tax invoices within an unclear statutory framework where they cannot verify that the supplier’s annual turnover is below the legally prescribed threshold? Doesn’t that expose them to tax liabilities based on information they have no access to and that is the exclusive knowledge of the supplier?




Consequently, small-scale farmers and small trading operations are finding themselves subject to administrative actions that amount to unjustified interference that manifests as punitive assessments that charge them with noncompliance.




Going by paragraph 5(2) of the 

Tax Procedures (Electronic Tax Invoice) Regulations

 of 2024, taxpayers face further challenges because the existing process for notifying the KRA whenever the system is not working is impracticable and shifts the burden or consequences of a failed digital platform onto taxpayers.




In effect, a taxpayer is expected to “a) notify the Commissioner in writing within twenty-four hours of the user’s inability to use the system; and b) record sales using any other means as may be specified by the Commissioner” if they’re having problems using the system.




Additionally, the appeals timelines become unreasonable when businesses cannot use the relevant system functions because of connectivity problems, technology capabilities, or disruptions caused by lack of access to system components that are experiencing outages, while other capacities are accessible, functional, and working. 




As highlighted by Professor Akech, in the eyes of the public, most KRA failures can be attributed to the misapplication of discretionary powers or their outright abuse. This is made worse by the fact that the KRA does not seem to be obligated to respond within a reasonable timeframe to the satisfaction of taxpayers.




Hence, KRA acts in a high-handed manner that renders its processes excessively demanding and costly. This is even more painfully so when one is faced with long and winding judicial interventions when seeking redress. 




Ultimately, the efforts of the Ministry of Finance and the National Treasury to review the National Tax Policy should also consider how to establish guardrails around these powers to ensure that their application is legitimate.

author: Mwangi Githahu
title: Kenya-US Relations: What the Immediate Future May Hold Under New Envoy
content:
A Sesotho proverb says, “Those who eat people, cry; those who eat a crocodile, laugh.” This proverb shows that reactions and alignments shift entirely based on whose interests are affected (we grieve when our friends are harmed, but rejoice when an adversary is neutralized).




Conversely, Lord Palmerston, a 19th-century Anglo-Irish nobleman and statesman who was UK prime minister, is reported to have said, “We have no eternal allies, and we have no perpetual enemies. Our interests are eternal and perpetual, and those interests it is our duty to follow.”

title: Uganda: The Entrenchment of a Hereditary Military Oligarchy
content:
Uganda is approaching one of the most precarious political transitions in its post-independence history. The likely trajectory is not democratic consolidation but the slow institutionalization of a hereditary military oligarchy. Four developments are driving this shift: President Yoweri Museveni’s advanced age; the elevation of his son, Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, to Chief of Defence Forces (CDF); the operationalization of the Patriotic League of Uganda (PLU) as a parallel mobilization vehicle; and the legal entrenchment of military authority over civilian institutions. Taken together, these amount to what might be called a “slow-motion coup” already under way.




The most probable outcome is best described as contested dynastic authoritarianism, a system in which elections continue to serve as instruments of international legitimacy, while substantive power is contested within the first family and the military elite rather than at the ballot box. The formal opposition faces structural decapitation through repression and co-optation. Yet two under-examined institutions – the Anglican and Catholic Churches, and segments of Uganda’s Muslim community – offer potential, if imperfect, nonviolent pathways for mediation or resistance over the coming decade, complicated by the risk of Muslim youth radicalization.




A conventional, extra-constitutional military coup remains possible even as the regime works to secure de facto military dominance through promotions, strategic retirements of senior officers, legislative amendment, and patronage. The PLU’s grassroots strategy is designed to insulate the succession from exactly this risk, cultivating broad loyalty and framing dynastic continuity as patriotic inevitability rather than rupture. The principal danger to the plan, accordingly, lies less in popular revolt than in intra-elite fracture or palace intrigue should the succession falter.




Anatomy of a slow-motion coup




The regime has moved beyond personalist autocracy toward a durable, self-perpetuating system built on four pillars: fusion of military command with the first family, political mobilization through the PLU, subordination of parliament, and kleptocratic control of the state’s resources.




Uganda’s slide toward dynastic rule no longer needs to be projected; it can be observed directly. In 2024, Museveni handed his son the office of Chief of Defence Forces, together with an unusual personal grant of authority to promote senior officers – a clear departure from the constitutional design of a professional military answerable to civilian rather than familial command. Muhoozi has used this platform expansively, maintaining an active, often combative social media presence, intervening openly in partisan disputes, and, in June 2026, ordering troops to shut down Nation Media Group’s operations after critical coverage of his conduct. He has also directly ordered the arrest of opposition lawyer Erias Lukwago and the deportation of Kenyan lawyer Martha Karua, both members of Dr Kizza Besigye’s defence team – a signal that the regime now treats defence counsel, and not only defendants, as targets. In his national address of 4 July 2026, President Museveni appeared to defend his son’s actions, placing blame on Besigye for allegedly delaying court proceedings.




The institutional scaffolding around Muhoozi has matured alongside his personal profile. The Patriotic League of Uganda, rebranded in 2024 from an informal network of birthday rallies and fan clubs known as the “Muhoozi Project”, now runs village-level structures, community clean-up campaigns, and youth roadshows, and openly courts the same rural base the National Resistance Movement (NRM) has cultivated for four decades. It functions less as a political party than as an insurance policy: it absorbs potential rivals into patronage, builds a loyalty network running parallel to the NRM’s own, and softens the ground for a hereditary handover by presenting it as continuity rather than rupture. Leadership changes, such as the appointment of Hon. Fadil Twaha as Secretary General, signal a deliberate effort to deepen outreach among Muslim communities that feel marginalized in the League’s rise.




The 12

th

 Parliament offered an early demonstration of the PLU’s reach. The League withdrew its earlier backing for then Speaker Anita Among and her deputy, Thomas Tayebwa, clearing the way for Jacob Oboth-Oboth’s election as Speaker – a small but telling exercise of veto power over who leads the legislature, and a preview of the League’s capacity to install loyalists across institutions.




Legally, the UPDF (Amendment) Act of 2025 extends military court jurisdiction over civilians in cases the state characterizes as “military-related”, notwithstanding a 2025 Supreme Court ruling that had found such trials unconstitutional. Combined with the expansion of the Special Forces Command (SFC), increasingly described, including by critics within the security establishment itself, as an “army within the army” answering more to the first family than to ordinary UPDF command structures, the Act gives the regime a legal and coercive apparatus that operates semi-independently of civilian oversight. Documented abuses under this arrangement include SFC-linked abductions and the June 2026 closure of Nation Media Group’s outlets, enforced by troops besieging the premises.




The kleptocratic nexus




Corruption in Uganda has evolved from individual graft into systemic state capture. Research on the subject describes an elite cartel in which opaque networks connect state institutions to politically connected non-state actors, extending well beyond personal enrichment to become a primary instrument of political survival and regime consolidation. Anti-corruption bodies manage rather than eliminate graft, selectively prosecuting defectors while protecting the core of the first family’s financial empire. The proceeds fund the patronage network that keeps the NRM’s base compliant. To obscure this dynamic, the PLU has positioned itself publicly as the vanguard of an anti-corruption agenda within the emerging Muhoozi order.




Neutralization of the opposition




The incarceration of Dr Kizza Besigye on treason charges along with hundreds of opposition activists, the rearrest/disappearance of Muwanga Kivumbi and, notably, the apparent exile of Robert Kyagulanyi (Bobi Wine), Ibrahim Ssemujju Nganda, Winnie Kiiza, Lina Zedriga, and many other less known opposition activists, mark a strategic shift from managing the opposition to eliminating it as an effective force. Critically, the regime does not merely suppress opposition; it simulates it. Museveni has long been credited with “creating and controlling his own opposition”, rendering the formal electoral contest a controlled exercise designed to absorb Western criticism while demobilizing grassroots energy.




The silent pillars: The Church and the Mosque




The Anglican and Catholic churches




The Anglican Church of Uganda and the Roman Catholic Church remain the country’s largest civil society infrastructure, and both are entangled with State House patronage; bishops appear regularly as guests at state functions, and the churches have served as vehicles for the regime’s social-conservative agenda, most visibly the Anti-Homosexuality Act. That entanglement is real but not absolute. Archbishop Stephen Kaziimba Mugalu has periodically issued pastoral letters critical of state violence and corruption, calibrated to avoid direct confrontation but sufficient to establish that the institution retains an independent voice. Gen. Muhoozi’s own brand of assertive, at times messianic, Christian nationalism complicates this relationship rather than strengthening it; bishops comfortable with general rhetoric about a “Christian nation” are considerably less comfortable with a military strongman who claims a personal, unmediated covenant with Christ – a claim that implicitly bypasses church authority.




The Catholic hierarchy, organised through the Uganda Episcopal Conference (UEC), has generally been the more outspoken of the two. It condemned electoral violence and voter intimidation after the 2021 general election and subsequent by-elections, criticized the militarization of politics and the extension of military court jurisdiction under the 2025 UPDF Amendment Act, and, through figures such as Archbishop Paul Ssemogerere of Kampala, has addressed corruption, land grabbing, and state violence in pastoral letters that tend to be more pointed than most Protestant statements. In response to the arrest of opposition lawyers, including members of Erias Lukwago’s team, Catholic voices have specifically emphasized the right to legal representation and due process. This posture has roots in the Church’s role sheltering dissidents and documenting abuses during the Amin and Obote II periods – a legacy that gives its current interventions an institutional memory and credibility a newer or more state-aligned body would lack. Catholic statements also tend to be more systematically coordinated through the UEC and more focused on structural issues such as judicial independence, poverty, and youth marginalization, which has earned the Church respect among pro-democracy activists even as it draws accusations of “meddling in politics” from regime supporters.




Gen. Muhoozi’s public claims of divine visions and a special covenant with Jesus Christ create a specific unease within the established Church hierarchy. While bishops support the general notion of a “Christian nation”, they are wary of a political leader claiming a direct, unmediated divine mandate that bypasses the Church’s own institutional authority. In the near term, the Church is likely to remain a stabilizing force in any transition from Museveni to Muhoozi, since preventing chaos is a core institutional instinct. In the medium term (2032–2036), however, if Muhoozi’s governance mirrors the erratic tone of his public statements, the Church could become the most likely venue for elite defection from the regime’s moral consensus – and, in a post-Museveni scenario marked by excessive brutality, the only institution with both the moral authority and the physical reach to mediate a nonviolent transfer of power or demand accountability.




The Muslim community: Patronage, schism, and risk




Uganda’s Muslim community, roughly 16 to 20 per cent of the population, is simultaneously one of the regime’s more reliable constituencies and one of its more persistent sources of anxiety. Museveni’s outreach to this constituency has become markedly more systematic – and more personally transactional – than earlier accounts of “institutional co-optation” suggest. The clearest evidence lies in the president’s direct sponsorship of Hajj and Umrah pilgrimages – run out of State House rather than through any independent religious charity. In July 2025, Museveni fully funded Umrah travel to Mecca for fifty Ugandan Muslims – imams, sheikhs, and sheikhas selected through local Muslim leadership structures – at a Kampala ceremony where State House officials framed the gesture explicitly as the revival of an earlier presidential pledge. The same event announced a plan to capitalize Imam SACCOs (Sharia-compliant savings and credit cooperatives) with 100 million Ugandan shillings each across 125 districts, giving otherwise unsalaried imams a direct financial stake in the president’s continued goodwill.




Ten months later, in May 2026, the programme scaled up sharply: Museveni sponsored 150 pilgrims for the full Hajj, up from a usual allocation of around 100, at a cost State House officials put at over three billion shillings, with selection again routed through the Uganda Muslim Supreme Council (UMSC) and coordinated by presidential aides including Moses Byaruhanga and Hajjat Mariam Namayanja. Pilgrims interviewed at the flag-off ceremonies were unambiguous about the transactional framing of the programme; they described receiving an Umrah offer one year and a Hajj slot the next, thanked the president by name rather than the state, and were explicitly warned by his aides against paying anyone else for assistance – a warning that doubles as a reminder of exactly who controls access to the programme. Because the Hajj and Umrah are religious obligations many rural and working-class Ugandan Muslims could never otherwise afford, presidential sponsorship converts a spiritual milestone into a personal debt of gratitude owed to Museveni individually, channelled through the UMSC’s Old Kampala leadership under Mufti Sheikh Shaban Ramadhan Mubaje.




This mechanism sits alongside, rather than replaces, other tools of co-optation: Parish Development Model (PDM) funding routed through UMSC structures, public pledges of loyalty from Muslim leaders at NRM rallies, and the positioning of UMSC as the state’s preferred interlocutor for the entire Muslim community. The cumulative effect is to make Old Kampala’s leadership a conveyor belt for regime legitimacy among Muslims – a mechanism that is more granular and more personal than “institutional co-optation” alone conveys, running through named individuals receiving named gifts at named ceremonies, repeated annually as a renewable incentive rather than a one-off gesture.




The Kibuli faction, tracing its independence to the legacy of Prince Badru Kakungulu and now nominally led by his son, Prince Kassim Nakibinge, together with the appointed Supreme Mufti, Sheikh Galabuzi, remains the structural counterweight to Old Kampala. It has largely stayed outside the Hajj-and-SACCO patronage circuit, preserving its credibility with opposition figures who seek Muslim legitimacy without the taint of State House sponsorship – a pattern visible in the tendency of opposition leaders to visit Kibuli rather than Old Kampala. That independence is also why Kibuli, and independent Salafi-leaning clerics more broadly, would carry disproportionate weight in any scenario involving elite fracture or popular unrest; they are not bound by the same web of state favours.




Muslim youth radicalization remains a real risk, and arguably an underpriced one, given a patronage strategy focused on senior clerics rather than on the young men most exposed to radical recruitment in Kampala and other urban slums especially in Eastern Uganda. Longstanding grievances over political and economic marginalization, unresolved land disputes, and a string of unsolved clerical assassinations since the mid-2010s have bred resentment that Hajj sponsorships for sheikhs do little to address, since the beneficiaries are disproportionately older, established religious leaders. 




The Allied Democratic Forces (ADF), though now largely a DRC-based Islamic State affiliate, originated among disaffected Muslim Tabligh youth in the 1990s, and the security establishment’s institutional memory of that history means any independent Muslim youth mobilization in areas such as Bwaise or Kisenyi is watched warily rather than engaged constructively. Gen. Muhoozi’s overtly Christian nationalist public persona widens rather than narrows this gap: a president who mixes ecumenical courtesy with personal favour is, in Muslim eyes, a different proposition from a Chief of Defence Forces who speaks of a personal covenant with Christ.




Under a Muhoozi presidency characterized by Christian nationalist rhetoric, the current arrangement with Old Kampala’s leadership may become a depreciating asset. The community could face sharper economic and political marginalization, transforming independent factions or radicalized fringes into sources either of nonviolent civil resistance – framed in terms of Islamic economic justice – or, in the worst case, of violent extremism that complicates dynastic stability.




Scenario projections: The next ten years (2026–2036)




Scenario 1: The managed succession (most likely, 50 per cent probability)




Museveni contests and “wins” the 2031 election. The real action occurs in the barracks as Gen. Kainerugaba purges the UPDF of officers loyal to the old NRA ideology rather than the family. Parliament, filled with NRM members who now openly carry the Patriotic League of Uganda (Muhoozi’s political vehicle) emblem, ratifies this transition. PLU structures and the UPDF Amendment Act provide legal and mobilization cover.




Faith Sector Role: Both Old Kampala UMSC and the Anglican hierarchy issue statements calling for “calm and continuity”, effectively blessing the dynastic transfer – though Muslim radicalization risks may simmer beneath the surface.




Scenario 2: The palace coup or fracture (likely, 15 per cent probability)




This scenario hinges on Gen. Kainerugaba’s volatile temperament. A premature push by Muhoozi to oust his father, or a miscalculation in handling internal NRM dissent, could trigger a violent split within the security forces. This is the “Warrior-Mad-King” scenario. In this chaos, the opposition would be a spectator, but the religious institutions would become critical. The Church and independent Muslim voices (including Kibuli) would be the only neutral ground available for emergency dialogue between warring UPDF factions, while Salafi discontent could complicate resolution.




Scenario 3: Systemic collapse – Anti-Museveni-Muhoozi military coup and popular uprising (like, 15 per cent probability)




This wild card requires economic turmoil to align with a moment of military elite fracture and a specific social trigger (e.g. a sharp currency devaluation combined with a widely condemned act of brutality by SFC guards).




In this scenario, the Church’s lower clergy (parish priests) and independent imams in urban slums, potentially including radicalized Muslim elements, could provide the moral sanction for support to even a precarious military coup, hence increasing its chances of success and civil disobedience, echoing the role of the Church in the 1980s anti-Amin resistance or the 2011 “Walk to Work” protests.




Scenario 4: The late Museveni counter-purge (likely, high risk – 15–20 per cent probability)




In this scenario, an ageing but still shrewd President Museveni perceives a premature power grab by Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba and the Patriotic League of Uganda (PLU). Alarmed by PLU’s expanding influence in parliament, the NRM, and the UPDF, and fearing his son’s volatile temperament could force a dynastic transition while he is alive, Museveni acts decisively. He demotes Muhoozi from Chief of Defence Forces, initiates targeted purges of PLU-aligned officers and politicians, and elevates anti-Muhoozi elements within the old NRA guard, military intelligence, and NRM veterans. Using his intelligence networks, Museveni identifies and neutralizes key sympathizers through retirements, reshuffles, and selective prosecutions framed as anti-corruption or loyalty drives.




Tactically, Museveni secures quiet support – or at least neutrality – from opposition figures who view Muhoozi as a greater long-term threat, creating a temporary “anyone but Muhoozi” alignment. Parliament ratifies the moves under NRM majorities, while state media portrays them as necessary for stability and party discipline.




Feasibility and consequences: Museveni’s deep patronage networks and formal authority as Commander-in-Chief give him a strong chance of short-term success. However, the risks are substantial. Muhoozi’s loyalists in the Special Forces Command and younger officer corps could resist, triggering limited mutinies or underground sabotage. PLU structures, already embedded in grassroots mobilization, might fuel protests or defections, fracturing the ruling coalition. Economic volatility or a heavy-handed crackdown could spark urban unrest, with lower clergy and independent imams providing moral cover for dissent – echoing historical protest roles.




In the best case, Museveni reasserts dominance and delays succession. In the worst, the purge accelerates elite fractures, pushing the country toward Scenario 2 or 3 dynamics: open military splits, popular uprisings, or chaotic power vacuums. This scenario underscores the regime’s personalization – where one man’s survival instincts could either stabilize or unravel decades of carefully managed authoritarian continuity.




In this scenario, the faith sector would play a complex, dual-edged role shaped by calls for stability versus grassroots discontent. The Anglican hierarchy and Old Kampala UMSC would likely issue measured statements emphasizing “national unity, peace, and constitutional order”, effectively providing moral cover for Museveni’s counter-purge as a defence against chaos and dynastic adventurism. Senior religious leaders, many with longstanding ties to the state, would prioritize continuity and quietly endorse the moves as necessary to prevent military fragmentation.




Conversely, lower-level clergy – particularly parish priests in rural areas and independent imams in urban areas and opposition-leaning communities – could become focal points of dissent. They might frame the purges as evidence of elite infighting and declining legitimacy, offering moral sanction for civil disobedience, prayer vigils, or quiet support for affected officers and politicians.




The opposition’s strategic conundrum




The opposition’s current strategy – participating in fraudulent elections, absorbing repression, and appealing to Western condemnation – is a closed feedback loop. To remain relevant over a ten-year horizon, the opposition must undergo a radical strategic pivot in at least four directions.




First, it must decouple legitimacy from the ballot box. The focus must shift from vote-counting to power building: prioritizing parallel, informal governance structures in urban slums and rural areas – community-based justice mechanisms, informal savings cooperatives, and alternative media ecosystems that operate below the security radar.




Second, it must rebuild the civil-military bridge. The near-exclusive focus on Gen. Muhoozi’s conduct should be supplemented with a covert, nuanced effort to engage mid-ranking UPDF officers, many of whom are already aware of resentment within the ranks over the preferential treatment and impunity enjoyed by the SFC and the first family. The opposition needs a narrative that distinguishes a “professional UPDF” from a “palace guard” in the SFC.




Third, the opposition must abandon treating the religious community as a monolith and pursue a genuinely two-track engagement. On the Christian track, direct engagement with Archbishop Kaziimba and the Catholic bishops should not seek political endorsement but a pastoral commitment to non-violence and the sanctity of life; a public statement from the Church hierarchy condemning extrajudicial killings during any transition period would meaningfully constrain the SFC’s operational freedom. On the Muslim track, the opposition should pivot away from the co-opted UMSC toward Kibuli and independent clerics, reframing its message from secular democratic theory toward Islamic economic ethics – casting regime corruption and marginalization as violations of principles of social justice around interest, land grabbing, and wealth concentration. This shift could both activate an existing base and address the underlying drivers of youth radicalization.




Fourth, the diaspora’s role must shift from funding election campaigns to funding underground organizational capacity: encrypted communication tools, emergency medical and legal aid for detainees, and an economic lifeline for Ugandan youth that bypasses state-controlled patronage.




To conclude, the next decade in Uganda is likely to be defined by the consolidation of a family dynasty, achieved through a combination of legal engineering, military reorganization, and patronage rather than a single dramatic rupture. The metric of success for the opposition must therefore change. Success is no longer winning the presidency in 2031; it is surviving, and maintaining organizational coherence, long enough to be the only credible alternative when the military family eventually fractures.




The faith institutions – the Church and the Mosque – are, for now, ballast for the regime’s ship. They are also, however, the only lifeboats currently on deck. In the turbulent waters of the Muhoozi succession, compounded by the risks of Muslim marginalization and radicalization, the opposition’s ability to navigate toward the neutral, moral harbour these institutions provide will determine whether it is swept away entirely or manages to stay afloat for the long, uncertain journey ahead. Without strategic engagement with both the pulpit and the minbar, and without a proactive response to the communal drivers of discontent, the opposition risks becoming a permanent, decorative feature of a hereditary military state.

title: The New Scramble for Africa
content:
Something important is happening across the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa. Wars that appear local are drawing in actors from increasingly far away. Ports built for commerce acquire military uses. Gold mined in conflict zones travels through international financial centers. Drones purchased abroad alter wars. Governments negotiate with foreign powers while those same powers cultivate armed groups or parallel authorities elsewhere.




Sudan, Libya, Ethiopia, Eritrea, Somalia, Somaliland and Yemen are usually discussed as separate crises. Look more closely and the connections become difficult to ignore. A

 

United Nations investigation

 found that forces aligned with Khalifa Haftar helped move Colombian fighters through Libya to support Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces. Sudanese gold travels toward the Gulf, while

 

Chatham House has documented

 the importance of the UAE to the regional gold economy. In western Ethiopia, a

 

Reuters investigation

 found a large training camp for fighters intended for the RSF, with reliable sources saying the UAE financed the facility and provided trainers and logistical support. 




These are not isolated developments. They point toward a changing system of power around the Red Sea.




What is emerging is not another Berlin Conference. Foreign governments are not openly dividing Africa into colonies, and African governments are not passive spectators. They bargain, invite investment, seek weapons and sometimes use outside powers against domestic or regional rivals. But something more than ordinary diplomacy is taking place.




One striking change is the growing importance of powers once treated as secondary actors in African geopolitics. The United Arab Emirates, Turkey and Israel do not possess the worldwide reach of the old European empires. Yet wealth, military technology, commercial networks and strategic geography allow these middle powers to exercise influence far beyond their borders.




They are also flexible about how that influence is exercised. A government can be the useful partner in one country, a paramilitary organization in another, a parallel authority somewhere else, and a commercial company across several of them. The relationship need not be ideological, and the partner need not even be a state. Strategic usefulness can be enough.




The UAE provides perhaps the clearest example. In Sudan, it has been supporting the RSF.




In Libya, it became an important external supporter of Khalifa Haftar’s eastern forces.

 

Reuters has documented

 earlier UN findings that the UAE helped Haftar’s forces build their air power, while Turkey supplied drones and air defenses to the government in Tripoli.




The Sudan and Libya stories have since begun to merge. The

 

UN Panel of Experts on Libya

 found that Colombian fighters transited through Haftar-controlled territory to support the RSF and described Libya as an operational, logistical and tactical base.




Gold reveals the economic side of the same system.

 

Chatham House

 describes gold as a major driver of Sudan’s conflict. Between 2012 and 2022, according to

 figures examined by Chatham House

, the UAE imported 2,569 tonnes of African gold that African countries themselves did not record as exports, worth approximately $115 billion.




The connection between gold and armed power is not abstract. The

 

U.S. Treasury

 sanctioned UAE-based companies connected to the RSF network. It said AZ Gold purchased Sudanese gold apparently for the benefit of the RSF and transported it to Dubai.




Money, weapons and military support can therefore move toward African conflicts while gold and other resources move outward. The old colonial economy required foreign administrators. The contemporary system does not necessarily need them. Governments, armed groups, mining companies, traders, port operators and financial intermediaries can perform different parts of the process.




A recent

 

Financial Times investigation

 traced a much wider Emirati expansion involving ports, mining, agriculture and infrastructure across Africa. A port can be a commercial asset, logistics hub, source of political leverage and, under different circumstances, military platform.




It is here that the idea of a new scramble for Africa becomes useful.




The old scramble sought possession of territory. The emerging one can operate at a distance. An outside power does not necessarily need to govern the mine, occupy the port or administer the population. It needs influence over the networks through which weapons, money, commodities and political power move.




We might call this long-distance colonialism. I use the term as a question rather than a label for every foreign relationship. Foreign investment is not colonialism. An arms sale is not colonialism. A port concession is not colonialism. The important question is what happens when these relationships accumulate, when investment becomes dependency, military assistance strengthens coercive power, and control over ports, resources or security begins narrowing meaningful sovereignty.




The Red Sea is one of the best places to ask that question because the Red Sea has two sides.




Analysis still tends to privilege the Arabian shore: Yemen, Saudi Arabia, Iran, Israel and the Houthis. Yet Eritrea, Sudan, Djibouti and Somalia possess the ports, coastlines and strategic locations without which Red Sea politics cannot be understood. Bab el-Mandeb does not separate these worlds. It connects them.




There is historical precedent. During the Cold War, the United States valued Eritrea partly because of Kagnew Station, its strategic communications facility in Asmara. Declassified

 

State Department records

 described American military assistance to Haile Selassie’s government as the quid pro quo for Kagnew. Haile Selassie understood American strategic interest in Eritrea and used it while Eritrean self-determination was being destroyed.




That history makes Ethiopia’s renewed campaign for the Red Sea especially important. The English word “access” makes the dispute sound almost innocuous. Commercial access to a port and sovereignty over territory are entirely different matters.




Ethiopia itself demonstrated the distinction after Eritrean independence. Under the

 

1993 Transit and Port Services Agreement

, Assab and Massawa were designated as transit ports for Ethiopian commerce. Ethiopian goods moving through them were exempt from Eritrean taxes and customs duties. Ethiopia could maintain offices and warehouses.




Ethiopia therefore does not need to own Assab to use Assab. Commercial access can be negotiated between sovereign states when relations are peaceful and based on trust. Territorial sovereignty is another matter entirely.




The issue became even clearer on October 4, when the leaders of Egypt, Eritrea, Sudan and Somalia met in New Alamein. Their

 

joint declaration

 reaffirmed sovereignty and territorial integrity, rejected recognition or support for Somaliland, supported Sudan’s territorial integrity and, most importantly, declared that governance of the Red Sea is the exclusive responsibility of littoral states.




Ethiopia was not named. It hardly needed to be.




Addis Ababa answered almost immediately. On October 5, after being sworn in for another term, Abiy again insisted that Ethiopia must obtain an outlet to the sea. Ethiopia’s Foreign Ministry argued that changing political boundaries do not erase Ethiopia’s historical connection to the Red Sea and insisted upon its “legitimate interests” and “enduring connection” to it.




The disagreement could hardly be clearer. Four states possessing the coastline say governance of the Red Sea belongs to littoral states. A landlocked state answers that proximity and national interest give it a legitimate place in the maritime order.




But proximity is not sovereignty. Geography can create economic and security interests. It does not create ownership of somebody else’s coastline.




The four states also appear to be moving beyond declarations.

 

Reuters reported

, citing Egyptian and other political officials, that Egypt, Eritrea, Sudan and Somalia agreed to coordinate military and intelligence efforts if Ethiopia’s conflict reaches its borders with Eritrea, Sudan or Somalia. That understanding does not appear in the published declaration, but it suggests that political coordination is acquiring a security dimension.




The geography explains why. Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea and Somalia form an African strategic arc stretching from the northern Red Sea through Bab el-Mandeb and into the Gulf of Aden. Sudan connects this system to the RSF war and Gulf competition. Eritrea possesses Assab and a long Red Sea coastline. Somalia confronts the Somaliland question and Ethiopia’s attempt to secure a coastal foothold through its memorandum with Hargeisa. Egypt brings the Nile dispute into the same strategic space.




This response also reminds us that Africans are not passive terrain upon which outside powers compete. But “African agency” should not become another abstraction. We need to ask which Africans possess agency, what they use it for and who pays the price.




That distinction is particularly important in Ethiopia. It would be misleading to describe Abiy Ahmed and the UAE simply as partners pursuing mutual national interests. The UAE has a broad regional strategy involving ports, logistics, minerals, and political influence. Abiy’s political calculus is much narrower. His overriding interest is remaining in power.




Ethiopia is not Abiy Ahmed, and his interests should not automatically be treated as Ethiopian national interests. His government has presided over devastating internal wars, displacement and the militarization of political disputes. Foreign money, weapons, drones, and diplomatic relationships can strengthen the government at the center while ordinary Ethiopians bear the consequences.




This is precisely how the new scramble can work. Outside powers do not need local partners who share their long-term objectives. They need partners who find the relationship useful. An outside power may want a port, minerals, military access or regional influence. A ruler receiving its support may primarily want the resources necessary to remain in power. They do not need the same objective. They only need to find one another useful.




Ethiopia’s Red Sea ambitions also intersect with outside military relationships. France agreed in 2019 to help landlocked Ethiopia rebuild a navy.

 

French government sources

 describe assistance in reconstructing Ethiopian naval capacity and training. There is an irony here. France has been pushed out of parts of West Africa while helping a landlocked government on the other side of the continent develop naval capabilities as that government increasingly asserts a strategic claim to the Red Sea.




Israel represents another variation. In December 2025,

 

Israel became the first country to recognize Somaliland

, despite Somalia’s objections and opposition from the African Union. Somaliland has subsequently acknowledged receiving Israeli military and police training. Israel has also publicly supported Ethiopia’s pursuit of maritime access.




These developments do not prove a single coordinated project among Israel, Ethiopia and the UAE. Their interests differ. But they show how local territorial disputes become intertwined with the ambitions of outside powers.




Turkey represents another form of influence. Turkish drones were among the foreign weapons that altered the earlier Tigray war.

 

Reuters reported

 that Washington raised concerns about Turkish armed drone sales to Ethiopia. Ankara did not need to occupy Ethiopian territory to become consequential. Military technology itself became an instrument of influence.




Russia provides another variation. Wagner developed relationships around mineral extraction and security in Africa, including Sudan’s gold economy, while Moscow has pursued a naval presence on Sudan’s Red Sea coast. Organizations and partners can change while the strategic objective survives.




This is not simply Africa versus outsiders. Saudi Arabia and the UAE compete. Turkey and Israel pursue their own relationships. African governments bargain, resist and change partners. What connects these developments is not a secret alliance but a method of exercising power.




Ports, drones, minerals, military training, diplomatic recognition, investment, paramilitary forces and political relationships can all become instruments within the same geopolitical system.




The African shore becomes even more important when instability affects other maritime routes.

 

Reuters reported on October 5

 that Eritrea’s roughly 1,000-kilometer Red Sea coastline is attracting renewed outside attention as conflict involving Iran raises concern about shipping through Hormuz.




This is why the Red Sea cannot be understood from the Arabian Peninsula alone. Hormuz, Yemen, Bab el-Mandeb and the African shore form one interconnected system. A disruption in one part changes the strategic value of another.




Geography can be a fortune for relatively poor countries. Strategic waterways, ports and coastlines can generate transit revenue, investment and bargaining power. But geography can become a curse when powerful actors decide that strategic value gives them entitlement. A commercially valuable port requires peace, insurance, predictable shipping and trust. A war fought to obtain a port could destroy precisely the economic value supposedly being sought.




The Houthis demonstrate another part of this changing order. They are commonly reduced to an Iranian proxy, although the movement predates contemporary Iranian support and emerged from Yemen’s own history. Yet they have demonstrated how a non-state actor positioned near a strategic chokepoint can acquire international influence vastly disproportionate to its conventional economic power. Geography, missiles, drones, and political organization can compensate for weakness.




Middle powers understand the same lesson. They do not need to dominate everywhere. They need leverage at particular nodes.




This is why long-distance colonialism is worth considering. The question is not whether every unequal relationship is colonial. It is whether apparently separate relationships are accumulating into something more durable: control exercised through networks rather than governors.




Who owns the infrastructure? Who finances it? Who controls the port or airfield during a crisis? Who supplies the weapons? Where do the minerals go? Who profits? Who makes the political decisions? And who bears the danger?




Those questions reveal something the conventional political map hides.




Sudan connects Gulf money and gold to western Ethiopia and Libya. Ethiopia’s confrontation with Eritrea connects its internal crisis to Assab and the Red Sea. Egypt connects Ethiopia’s regional confrontation to the Nile. Somaliland connects recognition politics to ports and military access. Yemen and the Houthis connect the African shore directly to Bab el-Mandeb. Russia seeks access on Sudan’s coast. France trains a navy for landlocked Ethiopia. Israel recognizes Somaliland and supports Ethiopia’s maritime ambitions. UAE networks cross several of these theaters.




Once these relationships are placed on the same map, they no longer look like unrelated crises. They form a connected but fragmented system of finance, weapons, commodities, political survival and strategic leverage.




The old scramble sought possession of African territory. The new scramble can be more flexible. It can seek ports without colonies, minerals without territorial administration, and military influence without permanent occupation. It can work through a president, a general, a paramilitary organization, a corporation or a port operator.




That may also explain why it is easier to overlook. The colonial flag has disappeared. The networks have not.




The decisive question is no longer simply whether foreign powers are present in Africa. They are. The more important questions are what their presence produces, which African actors benefit from it, whose power it strengthens, whose sovereignty it diminishes, and who ultimately pays the price.




The Red Sea has two sides, but the African side is rarely acknowledged.

title: Art is Maandamano
content:
In the weeks leading up to the storming of the Kenyan parliament in June 2024, I noticed a unique element in the type of people who attended the protests; they polled much younger, more enthusiastic, and some wore fairly pricey clothing. Not exactly what we have come to expect of Kenya’s rank-and-file rioters.




The quest for justice expressed through protest had found resonance with the type of Kenyan who would often be considered apolitical and indifferent to politics. They are not the group most invested in the mechanics of dealing with teargas, running battles, and placards. Something had changed, we just didn’t fully appreciate it yet. Somehow this apathetic regime had finally managed to enrage a unique, previously indifferent cluster: the middle-class Gen Zs.




In the heated political climate of mid-2024, Kenya witnessed an unprecedented wave of protests led largely by its Generation Z. While the immediate trigger was the controversial Finance Bill, the movement was distinguished not just by its scale but by its form. title: Finfinnee is the Third Space
content:
At the end of 2010, I took a trip to Ethiopia to visit my family. At the time, my parents worked in Bole, the commercial centre of Addis Ababa. Being only 16, my movements were more or less regulated by my parents, which meant that I would travel with them into the city each day, after which it was the extent of my curiosity and creativity (and pocket money) that determined what I did until evening, when I would head back to our house on the outskirts of the city. Slowly, interactions with the staff at a nearby cafe, just a few hundred meters from the building where my family worked, became routine. 




Over the two months that I was in Ethiopia, with much of this time spent in Addis Ababa, we spent most of our lunch breaks together, hanging out on the steps of the cafe, sharing stories to pass the time. One day, the conversation of our relationship to ‘Ethiopia’, as a national identity, came up. It’s important to note that I was raised in the Oromo diaspora, a community that, in the years my mother and I migrated to Australia, was made up mostly of political refugees who fled the country after the adoption of the “Transitional Period Charter of Ethiopia” and the official establishment of a transitional government.

author: Oyunga Pala
title: When Baba Died: One Year Later
content:
Last October, two weeks before Baba died, I was returning to Nairobi after a two-year hiatus. The last time I was home was during the first-year memorial of my sister, Nyangi, who was now the prominent character in my book.




Home had changed in many ways, yet it had not, in a kind of same old but different way. The vibe was familiar, the actors younger, the pace faster. Roads once familiar were now dwarfed by high-rise towers sprouting around the city like wild mushrooms. The expressway from the airport straddling the city dominated the cityscape, a marker of a city in a hurry to grow up.




I used to wonder whether I would change. Would I be like the other diaspora Kenyans I had seen who lost all sense of belonging after just a few miserable winters abroad, and began to look down on their own? Stepping away seemed to have had the opposite effect on me.

author: Chief Nyamweya
title: Art & AI: The End of Creativity or A New Era of Artistic Expression?
content:
The conversation around Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the creative industries is often filled with hype and speculation. Is it a tool for liberation or a threat to livelihoods? Chief Nyamweya, co-founder of the Kenyan animation studio Pungulu Pa Productions, cuts through the noise by sharing his on-the-ground experience developing the African children’s series

author: Reem Aljeally
title: Class, Creativity, and Cultural Production in Africa
content:
Artistic freedom and expression has long been shaped and constrained by many factors, including power, economic hierarchies, and class. In Africa, the right to create and distribute art without censorship has always been a contested terrain. Artists’ realities in the African region are directly influenced by both their geographical and societal positions; class plays a big role in how the art world runs. What does society consider as art?  Who gets to buy, collect, or even witness art?  Who has access to exhibition spaces or international residencies? These questions are not abstract; they define the careers of many artists, including my own.




Since 2011, we have seen youth-led movements harness creativity as a tool for political resistance, from the Arab Spring uprisings to #FeesMustFall in South Africa, #EndSARS in Nigeria, and, most recently, Kenya’s Gen Z protests. In Sudan, where I was born and raised, the December Revolution was marked not only by chants in the streets but also by murals, poems, songs, and performances that transformed the cityscape into a living archive of resistance. Yet, even within such moments of collective creativity, class distinctions determined who could participate, whose voices were amplified, and whose remained unheard.

author: Akingbade Tope Olatidoye
title: Humor Is Not A Joke: A Situation Analysis of Artistic Freedoms in Nigeria – A Cartoon Draws Blood!
content:
In March 2025, I posted a single-panel cartoon on a civic WhatsApp group that caricatured the Supreme Court: a judge in full wig, a smiling, hulking anarchical figure beside a broken gavel. It was meant as a provocation — a civic jab that asked whether a court’s public trust can survive repeated, controversial decisions.  In this case, I was questioning the role Nigeria’s apex court had played in preparing the illegal grounds for the unconstitutional suspension of the elected governor of Rivers State in the oil-rich Niger Delta region which had been the scene of many conflicts around resource control and rival politics. The reaction was immediate. Group messages ranged from sarcasm to outright threats. One respondent typed,  “Go commit a crime and let your case get to the Supreme Court — I want to check something.” 

The joke had not landed as a joke; it was a test. 




That exchange is not an isolated outrage; it’s a tiny weather vane. The barrage of abuse, the quick escalation from critique to menace, and the invocation of criminality as a retort reveal how fragile public satire has become.
