author: Benjamin Fogel
title: Brazil’s Racket Society
content:
Interview by William Shoki.




Brazil’s presidential election is headed for a runoff. In the first round on October 4, far-right Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, edged out President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva 47 percent to 45 percent. The right also consolidated its hold on Congress, with Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party now the largest bloc in the Senate. The result came despite Flávio’s thin record, his documented ties to Rio de Janeiro’s militias, and his father’s 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election.




As Latin America’s largest economy and its most populous democracy, Brazil has long served as a bellwether for the region, and increasingly for the world. Analysts of neoliberalism have used “Brazilianization” to describe a future of informal work, fortified elites, and hollowed-out states that they see arriving in the global North. The outcome of the runoff will help decide whether Brazil holds out against a regional turn toward Trump-aligned strongmen, a wave that has already swept Argentina, Ecuador, and, most recently, Colombia.




The stakes are high. Lula’s third term delivered growth, rising wages, and record-low unemployment, but it was hemmed in by a hostile Congress, and household debt and the cost of living kept climbing. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has intervened with unusual openness.

author: Jimmy Kitiro
title: Faith, Belonging, and the Kenyan Sacred
content:
In a 

recent edition

 of The Elephant, younger Kenyans voiced a growing dissatisfaction with the state of religion in public life. Their concern is not simply that religion has become political; it is that, in many instances, it has become too closely aligned with the state. Politicians continue to occupy pulpits, opaque fundraisers flourish, and a state-friendly theology often appears more concerned with legitimising power than confronting the hardship, corruption and inequality that shape ordinary Kenyan lives. During the 2024 Gen Z protests, this frustration crystallised in the #OccupyChurches movement, which challenged clergy and politicians who used religious spaces to legitimise unpopular economic policies and political authority.




Yet Kenya remains a profoundly religious country. The 2019 census found that about 85.5 per cent of Kenyans identified as Christian and 11 per cent as Muslim, and religious institutions still command large followings nationwide. Kenyans still flock to churches, mosques, crusades, prayer meetings and religious festivals, albeit for varied and sometimes contradictory reasons.

title: As Long as You Don’t Say Nothing, You Can Say Anything at All
content:
In Uganda, censorship is a reality, and in fact, a governance necessity. Once those governing us came to the realization that they cannot give the population what it needs, either because they don’t want to, or because they are not able, then they have got to try to stop the conversation about governing. Why permit or encourage talk about something you know is not going to change? Why raise hope?




That becomes step one, the usual result of which is to then see the discourse migrate to creative spaces, where it operates in a much more multi-layered and subliminal way. This requires a different kind of management of that arts scene, as step two.




With political censorship, matters have been very clear for some time now. Vocal activists who say things that those in power find offensive now have a standard playbook against them. They get barred from as many media outlets as they can. In extreme cases, landlords can be persuaded to evict them from their homes and business premises. Media houses themselves can be banned, or their troublesome journalists harassed or dismissed. Oftentimes, mass acts of violent rebellion primarily driven by youths are viewed as counterproductive and nihilistic. But it is important to note that this isn’t always the case, as three major examples in African contemporary history demonstrate notably: the anti-colonial theory of violence proffered by Frantz Fanon that galvanised Algeria into civil disobedience and warfare during the colonial era; the Arab Spring that gripped North Africa and parts of the Middle East in 2011; and the #RhodesMustFall movement that rattled South Africa in 2015.  Each of these instances of mass rebellion were largely youth-driven and shook the political status quo in their respective countries, leading to sociopolitical reform and fervent collective contemplation.

author: Olive Kobusingye
title: Medical Ethics and the State’s Security Interests
content:
I grew up on a staple of detective novels. Agatha Christie, Ian Fleming, P.D. James, Colin Dexter… there was always the smart forensics team that ultimately cracked the case. The dried blood stain nobody had noticed, the single hair on the comb, the fingerprints on the backdoor doorknob… I wanted to become a forensics expert when I grew up. Either that, or a psychiatrist. There was something fascinating about being able to read people’s minds, and to set them right if they were disturbed. I carried these thoughts with me into medical school.




The psychiatrist option suffered a rude jolt during the three weeks I spent on the psychiatry rotation as a junior clerk. It seemed as though the patients never got well. Most patients we met had been there before, several times. There were three, at most four, drugs that were used to treat all conditions. And then there was the electroconvulsive therapy, which left me persuaded that I did not want to return to that unit if I had the choice. I am glad things have changed tremendously since.




I went into internship with an open mind. Two weeks in, I was told I was on medico-legal duty. The assigned doctor did post-mortems and could be called upon to examine inmates at the municipal prison. These were usually convicts whose sentences included corporal punishment – caning.
